(a) Prohibition on Award of Contracts to Any Business Concern Owned, Controlled, or Operated by an Individual Convicted of a Felony.—
        (1) In general.—The Secretary of Homeland Security, acting through the Assistant Secretary of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement—
            (A) shall promulgate regulations establishing guidelines for the prohibition of contract awards for the provision of guard services under the contract security guard program of the Federal Protective Service to any business concern that is owned, controlled, or operated by an individual who has been convicted of a felony; and 
            (B) may consider permanent or interim prohibitions when promulgating the regulations.  
        (2) Contents.—The regulations under this subsection shall—
            (A) identify which serious felonies may prohibit a contractor from being awarded a contract; 
            (B) require contractors to provide information regarding any relevant felony convictions when submitting bids or proposals; and 
            (C) provide guidelines for the contracting officer to assess present responsibility, mitigating factors, and the risk associated with the previous conviction, and allow the contracting officer to award a contract under certain circumstances.   
    (b) Regulations.—Not later than 6 months after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary shall issue regulations to carry out this section.

fable.w: The section directs the Secretary of Homeland Security to promulgate and issue regulations, and under the definition a requirement of rulemaking counts as participation because rulemaking brings in public notice and comment. The tempting reading is that this is only an internal procurement rule involving federal officials and contract bidders, with no express comment period, hearing, or advisory body. That reading fails because the rulemaking mandate is itself enough to qualify.
fable.s: shall promulgate regulations establishing guidelines for the prohibition of contract awards for the provision of guard services under the contract security guard program of the Federal Protective Service

qwen_block.w: The section requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to promulgate regulations. According to the definition and Example 6, requiring or authorizing an agency to issue regulations constitutes participation because rulemaking typically involves public comment periods and other forms of public input. The text explicitly mandates the creation of these regulations.
qwen_block.s: shall promulgate regulations establishing guidelines for the prohibition of contract awards

opus.w: The section requires the Secretary of Homeland Security to issue regulations, both under subsection (a)(1)(A) and under the 6-month deadline in subsection (b). Under the definition, requiring rulemaking counts as participation, because rulemaking brings in public comment from people outside the government. One could read this as just a contract-eligibility rule, where bidding for contracts is not participation. But that reading ignores the regulation requirement, which meets the definition on its own.
opus.s: (b) Regulations.—Not later than 6 months after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary shall issue regulations to carry out this section.
opus.b: The tempting reading is that this is only about contract eligibility. Contract bids are a "No" trap, and the Secretary, ICE and the contracting officer are all inside the federal government. That reading misses the definition's explicit rule that requiring rulemaking counts as participation, as Example 6 shows. Here the Secretary is required to promulgate regulations.

qwen_chat.w: This section mandates the creation of regulations governing the award of contracts. The requirement for contractors to submit information and the assessment of their responsibility are part of the bidding and application process for government contracts. The definition explicitly excludes 'applications for benefits, grants, contracts, or licenses' from the scope of participation. Therefore, this intra-governmental regulatory process regarding contract awards does not constitute participation by outside parties in federal decision-making.
qwen_chat.s: (B) require contractors to provide information regarding any relevant felony convictions when submitting bids or proposals; and (C) provide guidelines for the contracting officer to assess present responsibility, mitigating factors, and the risk associated with the previous conviction, and allow the contracting officer to award a contract under certain circumstances.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the regulations require contractors to provide information and allow them to present mitigating factors, this constitutes participation. However, this is part of the application/bidding process for a contract. The definition explicitly states that "applications for benefits, grants, contracts, or licenses... applying for something is not participating in the decision." The interaction described is procedural compliance for a commercial transaction, not a mechanism for outside parties to consult on or influence federal policy decisions.
